blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Every question in this exercise uses a few facts about the cube roots of unity \(1,\ \omega,\ \omega^{2}\): \(\omega=\frac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\) and \(\omega^{2}=\frac{-1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\); \(\omega^{3}=1\); \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\). Moving one term of the last fact to the other side gives \(1+\omega=-\omega^{2}\), \(1+\omega^{2}=-\omega\) and \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\). To reduce a big power \(\omega^{n}\), divide \(n\) by 3 and keep only the remainder: \(\omega^{3k}=1\), \(\omega^{3k+1}=\omega\), \(\omega^{3k+2}=\omega^{2}\). Also \(\sqrt{-3}=\sqrt{3}\,i\). If \(k\) is one cube root of a number, its three cube roots are \(k,\ k\omega,\ k\omega^{2}\).

blocks.prompt: 1 (i) Find the three cube roots of \(8\).
blocks.explanation: A cube-root question: we need every number \(x\) whose cube is the given number. Every non-zero number has three cube roots, one real and two complex. Plan: write \(x^{3}=a\) as an equation equal to zero, factorize it as a sum or difference of two cubes, solve the linear factor and the quadratic factor, then write the complex roots with \(\omega\).
steps:
Step 1: Turn the question into an equation
\[x^{3}=8\]
\[x^{3}-8=0\]
\[x^{3}-2^{3}=0\]
Why: A cube root of 8 is a number whose cube is 8. Writing it as "something = 0" lets us factorize; and \(8=2^{3}\).

Step 2: Factorize as a difference of cubes
\[a^{3}-b^{3}=(a-b)(a^{2}+ab+b^{2})\]
\[(x-2)(x^{2}+2x+4)=0\]
Why: Here \(a=x\), \(b=2\), so \(ab=2x\) and \(b^{2}=4\). If a product is zero, at least one factor is zero.

Step 3: The linear factor gives the real root
\[x-2=0\]
\[x=2\]
Why: Setting the first factor equal to zero gives the real cube root at once.

Step 4: Solve the quadratic factor
\[x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{-12}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{-2\pm2\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[x=-1\pm\sqrt{3}i\]
Why: \(x^{2}+2x+4\) has no real factors, so we use the quadratic formula with \(a=1,\ b=2,\ c=4\); and \(\sqrt{-12}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{3}\sqrt{-1}=2\sqrt{3}i\).

Step 5: Write the complex roots with omega
\[-1+\sqrt{3}i=2\cdot\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[-1+\sqrt{3}i=2\omega\]
\[-1-\sqrt{3}i=2\omega^{2}\]
Why: Taking the factor 2 outside leaves exactly \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\).

Check: cube each root
\[(2\omega)^{3}=8\omega^{3}=8\]
\[(2\omega^{2})^{3}=8\omega^{6}=8\]
Why: \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(\omega^{6}=1\), so both complex roots really cube to 8 (and \(2^{3}=8\)).
blocks.final_answer: The cube roots of \(8\) are \(2,\ 2\omega,\ 2\omega^{2}\), i.e. \(2,\ -1+\sqrt{3}i,\ -1-\sqrt{3}i\).

blocks.prompt: 1 (ii) Find the three cube roots of \(-8\). [The book prints this part as \(8\), the same as part (i); its answer key gives the cube roots of \(-8\). See the book correction below.]
blocks.explanation: A cube-root question: we need every number \(x\) whose cube is the given number. Every non-zero number has three cube roots, one real and two complex. Plan: write \(x^{3}=a\) as an equation equal to zero, factorize it as a sum or difference of two cubes, solve the linear factor and the quadratic factor, then write the complex roots with \(\omega\). Here the number is negative, so we use the sum of two cubes.
steps:
Step 1: Turn the question into an equation
\[x^{3}=-8\]
\[x^{3}+8=0\]
\[x^{3}+2^{3}=0\]
Why: A cube root of \(-8\) is a number whose cube is \(-8\); adding 8 to both sides makes the right side zero.

Step 2: Factorize as a sum of cubes
\[a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)(a^{2}-ab+b^{2})\]
\[(x+2)(x^{2}-2x+4)=0\]
Why: With \(a=x\), \(b=2\). Note the signs: plus in the first bracket, minus on the middle term of the second.

Step 3: The linear factor gives the real root
\[x+2=0\]
\[x=-2\]
Why: A negative number has a negative real cube root: \((-2)^{3}=-8\).

Step 4: Solve the quadratic factor
\[x=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{2\pm2\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[x=1\pm\sqrt{3}i\]
Why: Quadratic formula with \(a=1,\ b=-2,\ c=4\), so \(-b=2\); and \(\sqrt{-12}=2\sqrt{3}i\).

Step 5: Write the complex roots with omega
\[1-\sqrt{3}i=-2\cdot\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[1-\sqrt{3}i=-2\omega\]
\[1+\sqrt{3}i=-2\omega^{2}\]
Why: Taking \(-2\) outside flips every sign inside, which leaves \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\).

Check: cube each root
\[(-2\omega)^{3}=-8\omega^{3}=-8\]
\[(-2\omega^{2})^{3}=-8\omega^{6}=-8\]
Why: An odd power keeps the minus sign, and \(\omega^{3}=\omega^{6}=1\).
blocks.final_answer: The cube roots of \(-8\) are \(-2,\ -2\omega,\ -2\omega^{2}\), i.e. \(-2,\ 1-\sqrt{3}i,\ 1+\sqrt{3}i\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints part (ii) as \(8\), which only repeats part (i). Its answer key gives \(\{-2,\ -2\omega,\ -2\omega^{2}\}\) for (ii), and these are the cube roots of \(-8\); so the minus sign is missing in print and the intended number is \(-8\). We solved \(x^{3}=-8\). (Read as printed, the answer is the same as part (i): \(2,\ 2\omega,\ 2\omega^{2}\).)

blocks.prompt: 1 (iii) Find the three cube roots of \(27\).
blocks.explanation: A cube-root question: we need every number \(x\) whose cube is the given number. Every non-zero number has three cube roots, one real and two complex. Plan: write \(x^{3}=a\) as an equation equal to zero, factorize it as a sum or difference of two cubes, solve the linear factor and the quadratic factor, then write the complex roots with \(\omega\).
steps:
Step 1: Turn the question into an equation
\[x^{3}=27\]
\[x^{3}-3^{3}=0\]
Why: A cube root of 27 is a number whose cube is 27, and \(27=3^{3}\).

Step 2: Factorize as a difference of cubes
\[(x-3)(x^{2}+3x+9)=0\]
Why: \(a^{3}-b^{3}=(a-b)(a^{2}+ab+b^{2})\) with \(a=x\), \(b=3\).

Step 3: The real root
\[x-3=0\]
\[x=3\]
Why: One factor of a zero product must be zero.

Step 4: Solve the quadratic factor
\[x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{9-36}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{-27}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{-3\pm3\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
Why: Quadratic formula with \(a=1,\ b=3,\ c=9\); \(\sqrt{-27}=\sqrt{9}\sqrt{3}\,i=3\sqrt{3}i\).

Step 5: Write the complex roots with omega
\[\dfrac{-3+3\sqrt{3}i}{2}=3\omega\]
\[\dfrac{-3-3\sqrt{3}i}{2}=3\omega^{2}\]
Why: Take the common factor 3 out of the numerator: what remains is \(\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{3}i}{2}\).

Check: cube each root
\[(3\omega)^{3}=27\omega^{3}=27\]
\[(3\omega^{2})^{3}=27\omega^{6}=27\]
Why: \(\omega^{3}=\omega^{6}=1\).
blocks.final_answer: The cube roots of \(27\) are \(3,\ 3\omega,\ 3\omega^{2}\), i.e. \(3,\ \frac{-3+3\sqrt{3}i}{2},\ \frac{-3-3\sqrt{3}i}{2}\).

blocks.prompt: 1 (iv) Find the three cube roots of \(64\).
blocks.explanation: A cube-root question: we need every number \(x\) whose cube is the given number. Every non-zero number has three cube roots, one real and two complex. Plan: write \(x^{3}=a\) as an equation equal to zero, factorize it as a sum or difference of two cubes, solve the linear factor and the quadratic factor, then write the complex roots with \(\omega\).
steps:
Step 1: Turn the question into an equation
\[x^{3}=64\]
\[x^{3}-4^{3}=0\]
Why: A cube root of 64 is a number whose cube is 64, and \(64=4^{3}\).

Step 2: Factorize as a difference of cubes
\[(x-4)(x^{2}+4x+16)=0\]
Why: \(a=x\), \(b=4\): \(ab=4x\), \(b^{2}=16\).

Step 3: The real root
\[x-4=0\]
\[x=4\]
Why: First factor equal to zero.

Step 4: Solve the quadratic factor
\[x=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{16-64}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{-4\pm\sqrt{-48}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{-4\pm4\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[x=-2\pm2\sqrt{3}i\]
Why: Quadratic formula with \(a=1,\ b=4,\ c=16\); \(\sqrt{-48}=\sqrt{16}\sqrt{3}\,i=4\sqrt{3}i\).

Step 5: Write the complex roots with omega
\[-2+2\sqrt{3}i=4\cdot\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[-2+2\sqrt{3}i=4\omega\]
\[-2-2\sqrt{3}i=4\omega^{2}\]
Why: \(4\times\frac{-1}{2}=-2\) and \(4\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=2\sqrt{3}\).

Check: cube each root
\[(4\omega)^{3}=64\omega^{3}=64\]
\[(4\omega^{2})^{3}=64\omega^{6}=64\]
Why: \(\omega^{3}=\omega^{6}=1\).
blocks.final_answer: The cube roots of \(64\) are \(4,\ 4\omega,\ 4\omega^{2}\), i.e. \(4,\ -2+2\sqrt{3}i,\ -2-2\sqrt{3}i\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: For part (iv) the answer key prints \(\{-3,\ -3\omega,\ -3\omega^{2}\}\). Those are the cube roots of \(-27\) (since \((-3)^{3}=-27\)), not of the printed \(64\); the key's list for Question 1 fits the numbers \(8,\ -8,\ 27,\ -27,\ 64\), not the printed ones. The cube roots of \(64\) are \(4,\ 4\omega,\ 4\omega^{2}\).

blocks.prompt: 1 (v) Find the three cube roots of \(-625\).
blocks.explanation: A cube-root question again, but \(-625\) is not a perfect cube, so factorizing with whole numbers is awkward. Plan: find the one real cube root by splitting off a perfect cube (\(625=125\times5\)), then use the rule that the three cube roots are \(k,\ k\omega,\ k\omega^{2}\).
steps:
Step 1: Why k, k omega, k omega squared are all cube roots
\[(k\omega)^{3}=k^{3}\omega^{3}=k^{3}\]
\[(k\omega^{2})^{3}=k^{3}\omega^{6}=k^{3}\]
Why: Because \(\omega^{3}=1\), multiplying a cube root by \(\omega\) or \(\omega^{2}\) does not change its cube. The three numbers are different and a cubic equation has only three roots, so these are all of them.

Step 2: Find the real cube root
\[625=125\times5\]
\[\sqrt[3]{-625}=\sqrt[3]{-125}\cdot\sqrt[3]{5}\]
\[\sqrt[3]{-625}=-5\sqrt[3]{5}\]
Why: \(-125=(-5)^{3}\) is a perfect cube, and the cube root of a product is the product of the cube roots.

Step 3: The other two cube roots
\[k=-5\sqrt[3]{5}\]
\[k\omega=-5\sqrt[3]{5}\,\omega\]
\[k\omega^{2}=-5\sqrt[3]{5}\,\omega^{2}\]
Why: Apply the rule of Step 1 with \(k=-5\sqrt[3]{5}\).

Step 4: The same roots in the form a + ib
\[-\omega=\dfrac{1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[k\omega=\dfrac{5\sqrt[3]{5}}{2}(1-\sqrt{3}i)\]
\[k\omega^{2}=\dfrac{5\sqrt[3]{5}}{2}(1+\sqrt{3}i)\]
Why: \(k\omega=5\sqrt[3]{5}\cdot(-\omega)\) and \(-\omega\), \(-\omega^{2}\) are \(\frac{1\mp\sqrt{3}i}{2}\). Numerically the roots are about \(-8.55\) and \(4.27\mp7.40i\).

Check: cube the real root
\[(-5\sqrt[3]{5})^{3}=(-5)^{3}(\sqrt[3]{5})^{3}\]
\[=-125\times5=-625\]
Why: The cube of \(\sqrt[3]{5}\) is 5 by the meaning of a cube root; the other two follow from Step 1.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: For part (v) the answer key prints \(\{4,\ 4\omega,\ 4\omega^{2}\}\). Those are the cube roots of \(64\) (part (iv)), not of the printed \(-625\); the key has no answer for \(-625\). The correct cube roots of \(-625\) are \(-5\sqrt[3]{5},\ -5\sqrt[3]{5}\,\omega,\ -5\sqrt[3]{5}\,\omega^{2}\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Evaluate \((1+\omega-\omega^{2})^{8}\). [The book prints \((1+\omega-\omega)^{8}\); see the book correction below.]
blocks.explanation: An evaluation with \(\omega\): we must reduce the expression to a simple number using only \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\). Plan: first turn each bracket into a single term (or recognise it as \(\omega\) or \(\omega^{2}\)), then raise to the power, then reduce the powers of \(\omega\) by dividing by 3. Expanding an 8th power directly would be very long, so simplifying the bracket first is the key.
steps:
Step 1: Simplify the bracket
\[1+\omega-\omega^{2}=(1+\omega)-\omega^{2}\]
\[=-\omega^{2}-\omega^{2}\]
\[=-2\omega^{2}\]
Why: From \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\) we get \(1+\omega=-\omega^{2}\); then add the like terms.

Step 2: Raise to the power 8
\[(-2\omega^{2})^{8}=(-2)^{8}(\omega^{2})^{8}\]
\[=256\,\omega^{16}\]
Why: Power of a product: \((ab)^{n}=a^{n}b^{n}\). An even power of a negative number is positive: \((-2)^{8}=256\); and \((\omega^{2})^{8}=\omega^{16}\).

Step 3: Reduce the power of omega
\[\omega^{16}=(\omega^{3})^{5}\cdot\omega\]
\[\omega^{16}=\omega\]
Why: \(16=3\times5+1\), and \((\omega^{3})^{5}=1^{5}=1\).

Step 4: Result
\[(1+\omega-\omega^{2})^{8}=256\,\omega\]
Why: Put Step 3 into Step 2.

Check: reach the power 8 by repeated squaring
\[(-2\omega^{2})^{2}=4\omega^{4}=4\omega\]
\[(4\omega)^{2}=16\omega^{2}\]
\[(16\omega^{2})^{2}=256\omega^{4}\]
\[=256\,\omega\]
Why: Squaring three times gives the 8th power (\(2\times2\times2=8\)); the same answer comes out.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \((1+\omega-\omega)^{8}\). Taken literally this is \(1^{8}=1\). The answer key's \(256\omega\) shows that the intended bracket is \((1+\omega-\omega^{2})\): the square on the last \(\omega\) is missing in print. We solved \((1+\omega-\omega^{2})^{8}=256\omega\).

blocks.explanation: An evaluation with \(\omega\): we must reduce the expression to a simple number using only \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\). Plan: first turn each bracket into a single term (or recognise it as \(\omega\) or \(\omega^{2}\)), then raise to the power, then reduce the powers of \(\omega\) by dividing by 3.
steps:
Step 1: Reduce the two big powers
\[\omega^{28}=(\omega^{3})^{9}\cdot\omega=\omega\]
\[\omega^{29}=(\omega^{3})^{9}\cdot\omega^{2}=\omega^{2}\]
Why: \(28=27+1\) and \(29=27+2\); \(\omega^{27}=(\omega^{3})^{9}=1\), so only the remainders 1 and 2 matter.

Step 2: Use the main property
\[\omega^{28}+\omega^{29}+1=\omega+\omega^{2}+1\]
\[=0\]
Why: After reducing, the expression is exactly \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}\), which is 0.

Check: use the actual values
\[\omega+\omega^{2}=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}+\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
\[\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\]
\[-1+1=0\]
Why: The imaginary parts cancel and the real parts give \(-1\).

blocks.explanation: An evaluation with \(\omega\): we must reduce the expression to a simple number using only \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\). Plan: first turn each bracket into a single term (or recognise it as \(\omega\) or \(\omega^{2}\)), then raise to the power, then reduce the powers of \(\omega\) by dividing by 3.
steps:
Step 1: Simplify the first bracket
\[1+\omega-\omega^{2}=(1+\omega)-\omega^{2}\]
\[=-\omega^{2}-\omega^{2}=-2\omega^{2}\]
Why: \(1+\omega=-\omega^{2}\), as in part (i).

Step 2: Simplify the second bracket
\[1-\omega+\omega^{2}=(1+\omega^{2})-\omega\]
\[=-\omega-\omega=-2\omega\]
Why: Here group 1 with \(\omega^{2}\): \(1+\omega^{2}=-\omega\).

Step 3: Multiply
\[(-2\omega^{2})(-2\omega)=4\omega^{3}\]
\[=4\]
Why: Minus times minus is plus, \(2\times2=4\), and \(\omega^{2}\cdot\omega=\omega^{3}=1\).

Check: a second route, (1 + A)(1 - A)
\[A=\omega-\omega^{2}\]
\[(1+A)(1-A)=1-A^{2}\]
\[A^{2}=\omega^{2}-2\omega^{3}+\omega^{4}\]
\[A^{2}=\omega^{2}-2+\omega=-3\]
\[1-A^{2}=1+3=4\]
Why: The two brackets are \(1+A\) and \(1-A\); using \(\omega^{4}=\omega\) and \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\) gives the same 4.

blocks.prompt: 2 (iv) Evaluate \(\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{7}+\left(\frac{-1-\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{7}\). [The book prints the first bracket as \(\frac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\); see the book correction below.]
blocks.explanation: An evaluation with \(\omega\): we must reduce the expression to a simple number using only \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\). Plan: first turn each bracket into a single term (or recognise it as \(\omega\) or \(\omega^{2}\)), then raise to the power, then reduce the powers of \(\omega\) by dividing by 3. Here the brackets are \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\) in disguise.
steps:
Step 1: Recognise the brackets
\[\sqrt{-3}=\sqrt{3}\,i\]
\[\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}=\omega\]
\[\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{-3}}{2}=\omega^{2}\]
Why: With \(\sqrt{-3}=\sqrt{3}i\) the brackets match the values of \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\) exactly.

Step 2: Rewrite and reduce the powers
\[\omega^{7}+(\omega^{2})^{7}=\omega^{7}+\omega^{14}\]
\[\omega^{7}=(\omega^{3})^{2}\omega=\omega\]
\[\omega^{14}=(\omega^{3})^{4}\omega^{2}=\omega^{2}\]
Why: Power of a power multiplies the indices; \(7=6+1\) and \(14=12+2\).

Step 3: Add
\[\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\]
Why: From \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\).

Step 4: What the printed expression gives
\[\dfrac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}=-\omega^{2}\]
\[(-\omega^{2})^{7}+(\omega^{2})^{7}\]
\[=-\omega^{14}+\omega^{14}=0\]
Why: Taking a minus sign out of \(\frac{1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\) gives \(-\omega^{2}\); an odd power keeps the minus, so the two terms cancel. This is why the key's \(-1\) needs the first bracket \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\).

Check: conjugates
\[\omega^{14}=\omega^{2}=\overline{\omega}\]
\[\omega+\overline{\omega}=2\operatorname{Re}(\omega)\]
\[=2\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=-1\]
Why: A number plus its conjugate is twice its real part; the same \(-1\) comes out.
blocks.final_answer: \(-1\) (the expression exactly as printed, with \(\frac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\), equals \(0\))

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the first bracket as \(\frac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\), which is \(-\omega^{2}\); with it the sum is \(-\omega^{14}+\omega^{14}=0\). The answer key's \(-1\) is the value of \(\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{7}+\left(\frac{-1-\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{7}\), so a minus sign is missing before the 1. We solved the intended expression.

blocks.prompt: 2 (v) Evaluate \((-1+\sqrt{-3})^{5}+(-1-\sqrt{-3})^{5}\). [The book prints the first bracket as \((1+\sqrt{-3})\); see the book correction below.]
blocks.explanation: An evaluation with \(\omega\): we must reduce the expression to a simple number using only \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\). Plan: first turn each bracket into a single term (or recognise it as \(\omega\) or \(\omega^{2}\)), then raise to the power, then reduce the powers of \(\omega\) by dividing by 3. This is like part (iv), but without the division by 2, so the brackets are \(2\omega\) and \(2\omega^{2}\).
steps:
Step 1: Write each bracket with omega
\[-1+\sqrt{-3}=-1+\sqrt{3}i=2\omega\]
\[-1-\sqrt{-3}=-1-\sqrt{3}i=2\omega^{2}\]
Why: \(-1+\sqrt{3}i=2\cdot\frac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}=2\omega\); the same for the other bracket.

Step 2: Raise to the power 5
\[(2\omega)^{5}+(2\omega^{2})^{5}\]
\[=32\omega^{5}+32\omega^{10}\]
\[=32(\omega^{5}+\omega^{10})\]
Why: \(2^{5}=32\) and \((\omega^{2})^{5}=\omega^{10}\); then take 32 common.

Step 3: Reduce the powers and add
\[\omega^{5}=\omega^{3}\omega^{2}=\omega^{2}\]
\[\omega^{10}=(\omega^{3})^{3}\omega=\omega\]
\[32(\omega^{2}+\omega)=32(-1)\]
\[=-32\]
Why: \(5=3+2\), \(10=9+1\), and \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\).

Step 4: What the printed expression gives
\[1+\sqrt{-3}=-2\omega^{2}\]
\[(-2\omega^{2})^{5}+(2\omega^{2})^{5}=0\]
Why: \(1+\sqrt{3}i=-(-1-\sqrt{3}i)=-2\omega^{2}\); an odd power keeps the minus, so the two terms cancel. The key's \(-32\) needs \((-1+\sqrt{-3})\).

Check: conjugates
\[(2\omega)^{5}=32\omega^{2}\]
\[(2\omega^{2})^{5}=32\omega=\overline{32\omega^{2}}\]
\[\text{sum}=2\operatorname{Re}(32\omega^{2})\]
\[=64\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=-32\]
Why: The two terms are conjugates, so their sum is twice the real part.
blocks.final_answer: \(-32\) (the expression exactly as printed, with \((1+\sqrt{-3})\), equals \(0\))

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the first bracket as \((1+\sqrt{-3})\), which is \(-2\omega^{2}\); with it the sum is \((-2\omega^{2})^{5}+(2\omega^{2})^{5}=0\). The answer key's \(-32\) is the value of \((-1+\sqrt{-3})^{5}+(-1-\sqrt{-3})^{5}\), so a minus sign is missing before the 1. We solved the intended expression.

blocks.explanation: An identity: a statement true for all values of the letters. We must show the left-hand side (L.H.S.) equals the right-hand side (R.H.S.). Plan: start from the more complicated side (the one with \(\omega\)), multiply out, and remove \(\omega\) using \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\) and \(\omega^{3}=1\).
steps:
Step 1: Multiply the two omega brackets of the R.H.S.
\[(x-\omega y)(x-\omega^{2}y)\]
\[=x^{2}-\omega^{2}xy-\omega xy\]
\[\quad+\omega^{3}y^{2}\]
Why: Every term of one bracket times every term of the other; \(\omega\cdot\omega^{2}=\omega^{3}\).

Step 2: Remove omega
\[=x^{2}-(\omega+\omega^{2})xy+\omega^{3}y^{2}\]
\[=x^{2}+xy+y^{2}\]
Why: Take \(xy\) common from the middle terms; \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\) and \(\omega^{3}=1\).

Step 3: Multiply by the first bracket
\[(x-y)(x^{2}+xy+y^{2})\]
\[=x^{3}+x^{2}y+xy^{2}\]
\[\quad-x^{2}y-xy^{2}-y^{3}\]
\[=x^{3}-y^{3}\]
Why: Multiply \(x\) into the bracket, then \(-y\); the middle terms cancel in pairs.

Check: put x = 2, y = 1
\[\text{L.H.S.}=8-1=7\]
\[(2-\omega)(2-\omega^{2})\]
\[=4-2(\omega+\omega^{2})+\omega^{3}\]
\[=4+2+1=7\]
Why: With \(x-y=1\), the R.H.S. is the product of the last two brackets; both sides give 7.

blocks.explanation: An identity: a statement true for all values of the letters. We must show the left-hand side (L.H.S.) equals the right-hand side (R.H.S.). Plan: start from the more complicated side (the one with \(\omega\)), multiply out, and remove \(\omega\) using \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\) and \(\omega^{3}=1\).
steps:
Step 1: Multiply the two omega brackets, row by row
\[x(\ldots)=x^{2}+\omega^{2}xy+\omega xz\]
\[\omega y(\ldots)=\omega xy+\omega^{3}y^{2}+\omega^{2}yz\]
\[\omega^{2}z(\ldots)=\omega^{2}xz+\omega^{4}yz+\omega^{3}z^{2}\]
Why: Each term of \((x+\omega y+\omega^{2}z)\) multiplies the whole bracket \((x+\omega^{2}y+\omega z)\); nine products in all.

Step 2: Collect terms and remove omega
\[x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\]
\[+(\omega+\omega^{2})xy\]
\[+(\omega^{2}+\omega)yz\]
\[+(\omega+\omega^{2})zx\]
\[=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xy-yz-zx\]
Why: \(\omega^{3}=1\) and \(\omega^{4}=\omega\); each pair of like terms then has the coefficient \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\).

Step 3: Multiply by (x + y + z)
\[x(\ldots)=x^{3}+xy^{2}+xz^{2}\]
\[\quad-x^{2}y-xyz-x^{2}z\]
\[y(\ldots)=x^{2}y+y^{3}+yz^{2}\]
\[\quad-xy^{2}-y^{2}z-xyz\]
\[z(\ldots)=x^{2}z+y^{2}z+z^{3}\]
\[\quad-xyz-yz^{2}-xz^{2}\]
Why: Multiply \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) one at a time into \(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xy-yz-zx\).

Step 4: Add the three lines
\[=x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}-3xyz\]
\[=\text{L.H.S.}\]
Why: Every term like \(xy^{2}\) appears once with + and once with -, so it cancels; only the cubes and three \(-xyz\) remain.

Check: put x = 1, y = 0, z = 0
\[\text{L.H.S.}=1\]
\[\text{R.H.S.}=(1)(1)(1)=1\]
Why: Both sides agree; with \(x=y=z=1\) both sides are 0, since the R.H.S. then contains \(1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0\).

blocks.explanation: A long product to be shown equal to 1. Plan: reduce each power of \(\omega\), notice that the factors repeat as \((1+\omega)\) and \((1+\omega^{2})\), find the value of one pair, then count the pairs.
steps:
Step 1: Reduce the powers
\[\omega^{4}=\omega^{3}\cdot\omega=\omega\]
\[\omega^{8}=\omega^{6}\cdot\omega^{2}=\omega^{2}\]
\[\omega^{16}=\omega^{15}\cdot\omega=\omega\]
Why: The powers 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... double each time. Squaring \(\omega\) gives \(\omega^{2}\) and squaring \(\omega^{2}\) gives \(\omega^{4}=\omega\), so the reduced powers alternate \(\omega,\ \omega^{2},\ \omega,\ \omega^{2},\ldots\)

Step 2: Rewrite the product
\[(1+\omega)(1+\omega^{2})\cdot(1+\omega)(1+\omega^{2})\cdots\]
Why: The factors come in identical pairs.

Step 3: Value of one pair
\[(1+\omega)(1+\omega^{2})=(-\omega^{2})(-\omega)\]
\[=\omega^{3}=1\]
Why: \(1+\omega=-\omega^{2}\) and \(1+\omega^{2}=-\omega\); minus times minus is plus.

Step 4: Count the pairs
\[2n\text{ factors}=n\text{ pairs}\]
\[\text{Product}=1^{n}=1\]
Why: Each of the \(n\) pairs equals 1.

Check: n = 1 directly
\[(1+\omega)(1+\omega^{2})=1+\omega+\omega^{2}+\omega^{3}\]
\[=0+1=1\]
Why: Expanding the first pair without the shortcut gives the same 1.
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: the product of \(2n\) factors is \(1\).

blocks.prompt: 4 If \(\omega\) is a root of \(x^{2}+x+1=0\), show that its other root is \(\omega^{2}\) and hence prove that \(\omega^{3}=1\).
blocks.explanation: A question on the roots of a quadratic. For \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\) the sum of the roots is \(-\frac{b}{a}\) and the product is \(\frac{c}{a}\). Plan: write what "\(\omega\) is a root" means, use the sum of roots to find the other root, then the product of roots to get \(\omega^{3}=1\).
steps:
Step 1: What "omega is a root" means
\[\omega^{2}+\omega+1=0\]
\[\omega^{2}=-1-\omega\]
Why: A root makes the equation true when put in place of \(x\). We keep the rearranged form for Step 2.

Step 2: Find the other root from the sum of roots
\[\omega+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}=-1\]
\[\beta=-1-\omega\]
\[\beta=\omega^{2}\]
Why: Here \(a=b=c=1\). Calling the other root \(\beta\), Step 1 shows \(-1-\omega\) is exactly \(\omega^{2}\).

Step 3: Prove omega cubed = 1 from the product of roots
\[\omega\cdot\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}=1\]
\[\omega\cdot\omega^{2}=1\]
\[\omega^{3}=1\]
Why: The roots are \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\); multiplying powers adds the indices.

Check: omega squared satisfies the equation
\[(\omega^{2})^{2}+\omega^{2}+1=\omega^{4}+\omega^{2}+1\]
\[=\omega+\omega^{2}+1=0\]
Why: Using \(\omega^{3}=1\), \(\omega^{4}=\omega\). (Another route: \(x^{3}-1=(x-1)(x^{2}+x+1)\), so \(\omega^{3}-1=0\).)
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: the other root is \(\omega^{2}\), and \(\omega^{3}=1\).

blocks.prompt: 5 (a) [the book does not label the parts] Prove that complex cube roots of \(-1\) are \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\) and \(\frac{-1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\); and hence prove that \(\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}+\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}=-2\). [As printed; the statement has two misprints, see the book correction below.]
blocks.explanation: Two claims: what the complex cube roots of \(-1\) are, and the value of a sum of ninth powers. Plan: solve \(x^{3}=-1\) ourselves, compare with the printed roots, write the true roots with \(\omega\), and then work out the ninth powers. We will find that the printed roots and the printed first bracket are wrong, and prove the corrected statement.
steps:
Step 2: The real root and the complex roots
\[x+1=0\Rightarrow x=-1\]
\[x=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{1-4}}{2}\]
\[x=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{3}i}{2}\]
Why: Quadratic formula for \(x^{2}-x+1=0\) with \(a=1,\ b=-1,\ c=1\). So the complex cube roots of \(-1\) are \(\frac{1\pm\sqrt{3}i}{2}\).

Step 3: Test the printed roots
\[\left(\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\right)^{3}=\omega^{3}=1\]
\[\left(\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\right)^{3}=\omega^{6}=1\]
Why: The printed numbers are \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\); their cubes are \(+1\), not \(-1\). So they are cube roots of unity, and the printed claim cannot be proved.

Step 4: Write the true roots with omega
\[\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}=-\dfrac{-1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}=-\omega^{2}\]
\[\dfrac{1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}=-\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}=-\omega\]
\[(-\omega)^{3}=-\omega^{3}=-1\]
Why: Taking a minus sign outside flips every sign on top. The last line confirms \(-\omega\) really cubes to \(-1\) (and likewise \(-\omega^{2}\)).

Step 5: The ninth powers (corrected statement)
\[\left(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}=(-\omega^{2})^{9}\]
\[=-\omega^{18}=-1\]
\[\left(\dfrac{1-\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}=(-\omega)^{9}\]
\[=-\omega^{9}=-1\]
\[\text{Sum}=-1+(-1)=-2\]
Why: \(\sqrt{-3}=\sqrt{3}i\), so the brackets are the cube roots of \(-1\) from Step 4. An odd power keeps the minus; \(\omega^{18}=(\omega^{3})^{6}=1\), \(\omega^{9}=(\omega^{3})^{3}=1\).

Step 6: What the printed sum gives
\[\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}=\omega\]
\[\omega^{9}+(-\omega)^{9}=1-1=0\]
Why: With the printed first bracket the sum is 0, not \(-2\); the value \(-2\) needs \(\frac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\), which matches the corrected roots of Step 2.

Check: numbers
\[\left(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\right)^{3}=-1\]
\[\left(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\right)^{9}=(-1)^{3}=-1\]
Why: Cubing three times gives the ninth power; the same holds for the conjugate, so the sum is \(-2\).
blocks.final_answer: The complex cube roots of \(-1\) are \(\frac{1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\) and \(\frac{1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\) (that is, \(-\omega^{2}\) and \(-\omega\)); hence \(\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}+\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}=-2\). (With the printed first bracket \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\) the sum is \(0\).)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the complex cube roots of \(-1\) as \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\) and \(\frac{-1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\); those are \(\omega\) and \(\omega^{2}\), whose cubes are \(+1\). The correct complex cube roots of \(-1\) are \(\frac{1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}\) and \(\frac{1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}\). The book also prints the first ninth-power bracket as \(\frac{-1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\); with it the sum is \(1+(-1)=0\). The value \(-2\) is correct for \(\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}+\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{-3}}{2}\right)^{9}\).

blocks.prompt: 5 (b) Prove that \((-1+\sqrt{-3})^{4}+(-1-\sqrt{-3})^{4}=16\). [As printed; see the book correction below.]
blocks.explanation: We must find the value of a sum of fourth powers. Plan: as in Question 2 (v), write each bracket as \(2\omega\) or \(2\omega^{2}\), raise to the power 4, and reduce. The true value turns out to be \(-16\), not the printed 16.
steps:
Step 1: Write the brackets as 2 omega and 2 omega squared
\[-1+\sqrt{-3}=-1+\sqrt{3}i=2\omega\]
\[-1-\sqrt{-3}=-1-\sqrt{3}i=2\omega^{2}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{-3}=\sqrt{3}i\), and taking out the factor 2 leaves \(\omega\) or \(\omega^{2}\).

Step 2: Raise to the power 4 and reduce
\[(2\omega)^{4}+(2\omega^{2})^{4}=16\omega^{4}+16\omega^{8}\]
\[=16(\omega+\omega^{2})\]
\[=16(-1)=-16\]
Why: \(2^{4}=16\); \(\omega^{4}=\omega^{3}\omega=\omega\) and \(\omega^{8}=\omega^{6}\omega^{2}=\omega^{2}\); then \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\).

Check: direct expansion without omega
\[(-1+\sqrt{3}i)^{2}=1-2\sqrt{3}i-3\]
\[=-2-2\sqrt{3}i\]
\[(-2-2\sqrt{3}i)^{2}=4+8\sqrt{3}i-12\]
\[=-8+8\sqrt{3}i\]
\[(-1-\sqrt{3}i)^{4}=-8-8\sqrt{3}i\]
\[\text{Sum}=-16\]
Why: Squaring twice gives the fourth power; the second bracket is the conjugate, so its fourth power is the conjugate. The imaginary parts cancel and \(-8-8=-16\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book asks to prove \((-1+\sqrt{-3})^{4}+(-1-\sqrt{-3})^{4}=16\). The true value is \(-16\): the sum is \(16(\omega+\omega^{2})=16(-1)\). The minus sign is missing in print.

blocks.prompt: 6 If \(\omega\) is a cube root of unity, form an equation whose roots are \(2\omega\) and \(2\omega^{2}\).
blocks.explanation: We are given two roots and must build the quadratic equation. If the sum of the roots is \(S\) and the product is \(P\), the equation is \(x^{2}-Sx+P=0\). Here \(\omega\) means a complex cube root of unity (with \(\omega=1\) the roots would both be 2). Plan: find \(S\) and \(P\) with \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\) and \(\omega^{3}=1\), then substitute.
steps:
Step 1: Sum of the roots
\[S=2\omega+2\omega^{2}\]
\[=2(\omega+\omega^{2})\]
\[=2(-1)=-2\]
Why: Take 2 common, then \(\omega+\omega^{2}=-1\).

Step 2: Product of the roots
\[P=(2\omega)(2\omega^{2})\]
\[=4\omega^{3}=4\]
Why: Multiply the numbers and add the powers; \(\omega^{3}=1\).

Step 3: Form the equation
\[x^{2}-Sx+P=0\]
\[x^{2}-(-2)x+4=0\]
\[x^{2}+2x+4=0\]
Why: A quadratic with roots \(\alpha,\beta\) is \((x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=x^{2}-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta\).

Check: solve the equation
\[x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}\]
\[x=-1\pm\sqrt{3}i\]
Why: These are \(2\omega\) and \(2\omega^{2}\), exactly as found in Question 1 (i).
